howto.h1: Turn a product link into a video ad.
howto.lead: Paste one product URL — AI imports the photos and details for you, then turns them into a ready-to-post video. No camera, no filming, no editing timeline.

image.alt: Canvas tote bag product photo on a white background

intro: Most sellers start with one live product page and no video budget. URL to Video reads that page, keeps the title, the description and the photos you already published, and opens a prefilled product-demo draft. No camera, no clips.

The path suits a listing already good enough to sell from. If the photos are the weak part, improve them first. The importer can only work with what the page shows, so a thin listing produces a thin draft.

Nothing about the import is fixed in place. You correct the copy, choose the photo the video opens on, and describe the demo in your words. Building the draft costs nothing; the price of the video appears after you review it.

sections.h2: Where the link path saves time
paras: A working product page already answers what a script has to answer: what the item is, who it suits, and why a buyer would choose it. The importer turns those answers into the first draft, so you review instead of compose.

Take a different start when the page is not the bottleneck. A single strong shot moves faster through [Image to Video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video), and a product with no page yet belongs in [Text to Video](/guides/how-do-text-to-video). Sellers planning many videos keep every import in [Product Links](/guides/how-do-product-links) instead.

sections.h2: What the importer needs from the page
paras: The link must be public and served over https. Pages behind a login, a cart gate or a regional block do not open for the reader, and the tool returns a specific reason rather than a blank draft. That reason tells you what to fix.

Good input is a listing a stranger could buy from: a clear title, a description with real detail, and photos large enough to survive a vertical crop. One thumbnail and a single line of copy give the draft almost nothing to shape.
bullets: A page that opens in a browser without signing in.
A title that names the product rather than a campaign.
Photos big enough that the product still reads on a phone.
Variants written as text, not locked inside an image.

sections.h2: Checking what the import read
paras: The preview returns four things: the sourced title, the description, the images it detected, and a possible price. Each carries a confidence label, so you can tell a clean read from a guess. Read all four before you brief anything.

A possible price stays a hint and is never treated as confirmed. The reader may pick up a sale price, a variant price or a shipping line, and nothing checks it. If the ad shows a number, type the one you stand behind.

sections.h2: Confirming cost and starting the job
paras: One click on the imported entry opens the prefilled draft in the composer, with the photos, the description and the format settings already in place. Add a sentence of direction, then read the estimate.

A 15-second video costs 20 credits and a 30-second video costs 40. The confirmation modal restates that cost and your balance; confirming holds the credits. A failed job returns them, and the job runs on the server.

sections.h2: Where the finished video goes
paras: Finished work lands in the Library under All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed. The details modal shows the result, the per-shot clips, the description, every reference you attached, and the submitted duration, aspect ratio and resolution.

When one clip is wrong, pick the smallest repair. Try again re-runs a failed job, Retry render re-assembles clips that are already fine, and Regenerate prefills the composer from the job. Captions are a separate pass in [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio), and each pass saves a new version.

steps.title: Paste the product URL
steps.body: Open the live product page in a browser and copy the full address from the address bar. Paste it into the URL to Video field on Home. If the page cannot be read, the tool names the block.

steps.title: Review the imported photos
steps.body: The preview lists the title, the description, the detected images and a possible price, each with a confidence label. Open every thumbnail at full size. Keep the shots that show the product clearly, and choose the one the video opens on.

steps.title: Brief the video
steps.body: Write a sentence or two about what the product does, who it suits and where it is used. Fix any line the import got wrong, and retype the price if the ad shows one. The cost is visible before you commit.

steps.title: Confirm and generate
steps.body: The confirmation modal restates the estimated cost and your current balance. Confirming holds the credits and starts the job on the server. A failed job returns them automatically, and you can leave the page while it runs.

steps.title: Collect from the Library
steps.body: The job moves through generating, finishing and completed, and the Library badge updates when you come back. Download what you want to keep within 15 days, because finished videos expire after that, and a download carries no watermark.

steps.title: Fix the part that is wrong
steps.body: If the clips are fine and the assembly is not, use Retry render. If the direction was off, Regenerate prefills the composer from the job, so you change one thing rather than start over. Both keep the references you attached.

stepsIntro.title: Step by step
stepsIntro.lead: The loop matches the rest of the workspace: supply the source, review what was read, confirm a cost, then wait for a server job. The difference here is that a link carries the photos and the description for you.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: Guests can build the draft without an account, and it is restored the moment they sign in. Save as draft costs nothing, so compare two directions before spending credits.

checklist: The product page opens in a browser without signing in.
The description on the page matches what you actually sell.
You chose the shot the video opens on, not the first one listed.
The price in the copy is one you typed, not the imported guess.
You read the estimate before confirming, not after.

faq.q: Does the product page need anything special?
faq.a: It needs to be public and served over https. The reader takes the title, the description, the photos and a possible price from the page. A page behind a login returns a specific reason instead of a draft.

faq.q: What if the import picks a photo I don't want?
faq.a: Deselect it before you brief the video, then choose the shot the video opens on from the ones you keep. The video is built only from those photos. A wide lifestyle image often crops down to an empty frame.

faq.q: How much does one video cost?
faq.a: The composer shows the estimated credits before anything runs. A 15-second video costs 20 credits and a 30-second video costs 40, and the confirmation modal restates the cost and your balance. A failed job returns the credits.

faq.q: What happens to the price the importer found?
faq.a: It stays a possible price, marked with a confidence label, and it is never treated as confirmed. The reader can pick up a sale price, a variant price or a shipping line. Type the figure you want in the ad.

howto.h1: Bring one product photo to life.
howto.lead: Upload a single product photo and add a short prompt — watch the photo come alive as a moving product clip, ready for ads and social posts.

image.alt: Peachy tinted balm product photo on a marble vanity

intro: You already have the product photo. You need a few seconds where it moves: a hand lifting the bottle, a cap twisting open, light sliding across a label. Image to Video turns that photo and one action into a clip you can post.

The photo supplies the look: colours, surface, background. You supply the action in one short sentence. The camera drift, the pace, how firmly the product keeps its shape: the model decides. That is why the photo matters more than wording.

Upload, describe, confirm, compare: the loop is short and it repeats. Slow down on the first two, since a clean photo and one verb do more than any rewrite. If your product exists only as a page link, start with [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video).

sections.h2: What a single photo can do
paras: Image to Video suits products that read as one object: a balm tin, a tumbler, a folded shirt. The photo holds still while the model moves around it, so what you sell stays recognisable as motion arrives.

Some jobs want another tool. A page link is faster through URL to Video, which imports listing photos. Several angles in one longer story belong in AI Video, which takes up to four photos. A product that needs a speaker belongs in [AI Avatar](/guides/how-do-ai-avatar).

sections.h2: What makes a photo workable
paras: The composer accepts up to four product reference photos, and one is usually enough. The model needs a subject it can separate from its surroundings, so it moves the camera without smearing your product's edges.

Plain backgrounds win. A crowded shelf makes the model guess which shape is yours; a wall removes the guess. Even light keeps the label readable. A phone photo counts, since motion comes from your sentence, and the [product photo field guide](/guides/product-photo-tips) covers lighting in depth.
bullets: One product filling a third to half the frame.
Plain background, so nothing competes with the product.
Even light from one side so the label reads.
A phone shot at normal zoom, unfiltered and uncropped.

sections.h2: The quote before the job runs
paras: Before anything runs, the composer shows the cost. A 15-second clip costs 20 credits, a 30-second clip costs 40, and the figure changes with the duration. Set the length first, then read the line.

Choosing between them is a placement question. Fifteen seconds carries one beat for half the credits, which suits a test of a new angle. Thirty buys a second beat, a close-up then a use, if something real goes there.
The confirmation modal restates the estimated cost and your balance. Confirming holds the credits, and a failed job returns them automatically. The job runs on the server, so you can leave the page.

sections.h2: Reading the motion you got
paras: Watch the clip twice. First with sound off, as a scroller would meet it; then with your attention on the product. One pass says whether the motion reads, the other whether the label survived.

One motion per clip keeps results clean. Two actions in one brief, pick up and pour, split the model's attention and land neither. When a story needs both beats, make two clips and keep the stronger take.
When a result is close but wrong, a variation beats a rewrite. Change one thing, the verb, the photo or the duration, then compare both takes. Two changes at once hide which one fixed it.
bullets: Wrong action: rewrite the verb and regenerate the clip.
Odd pacing: try the brief at the other length.
Product deforming: swap the photo, not the sentence.
Flat framing: keep the take, change the angle later.

sections.h2: Where the clip goes next
paras: Finished videos wait in the Library, where All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed separate running jobs from ready ones. The badge updates while you are away. Download what you keep within 15 days.

The details modal lists the duration, aspect ratio and resolution you submitted, plus every reference you attached. If the clip needs words, [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio) works on completed videos and saves each pass as a version. Run the [review checklist](/blog/ai-video-review-checklist) first.

steps.title: Pick one strong photo
steps.body: Open the composer and add your product photo. Is the product fully in frame, is the background plain, is the light even enough to read the label? A phone shot that passes those three beats a studio shot that fails one.

steps.title: Describe one action
steps.body: Write one sentence with one verb: she lifts the bottle, the lid turns, the box slides open. Adjectives about mood add nothing the photo lacks. If you want a second beat, plan a second clip.

steps.title: Check the quote, confirm
steps.body: Set the duration to 15 or 30 seconds, then read the cost line, 20 credits or 40. The confirmation modal repeats that number next to your balance. Confirm only when it matches your plan; held credits return if the job fails.

steps.title: Compare and keep
steps.body: Generate a variation when the motion feels off, changing one input at a time. Watch both takes with the sound off and keep the one where the product stays recognisable. One clean take beats two near identical attempts.

steps.title: Collect it from the Library
steps.body: The job moves from generating to finishing to completed on the server, so you can leave the page. Check the submitted duration and resolution in the details modal, then download a copy to your own drive.

steps.title: Caption it if it needs words
steps.body: A moving product clip often works without speech, but a price, a size or a claim needs on-screen text. Subtitle Studio runs on completed videos and saves each operation as a new version, so the clean clip stays underneath.

stepsIntro.title: Six steps, one photo
stepsIntro.lead: The loop is short: one photo, one sentence, one confirmed job. Most of the thinking happens before you click, in choosing the photo and narrowing the action to a single motion.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: If the action feels wrong but the framing is right, change the verb before the photo. Rewriting one word costs less than reshooting and isolates the cause of a miss.

checklist: Product fully in frame on a plain or blurred background.
One verb in the action line, no second beat.
Duration chosen before you read the cost line.
Confirmation modal cost and balance matching what you expect.
Clip watched once with sound off before you download it.

faq.q: What kind of photo works best?
faq.a: One clear product, a plain background and even light. A phone photo is enough, since motion comes from the action you write rather than the source file.

faq.q: How long can the clip be?
faq.a: Choose 15 or 30 seconds when you set up the job. The composer shows 20 credits for fifteen seconds and 40 for thirty. Start short when testing a new angle.

faq.q: Can I use the clip in ads?
faq.a: Yes. Download the finished file from the Library with no watermark, then use it on your product page, in social posts and in paid ads. Publishing to TikTok or Meta takes one click.

faq.q: What happens if the motion comes out wrong?
faq.a: Regenerate with one change: a clearer verb, a cleaner photo or the other duration. Two takes show which input caused the miss. If a job fails, the reason is in plain language and the credits return automatically.

seo.twitterDescription: Type one sentence about your product — AI writes the script, scenes and shots.

howto.h1: From one sentence to a video brief.
howto.lead: Type one sentence about your product. AI writes the script and scenes, and turns it into an editable video brief — then generates the shots you choose.

image.alt: Review-style product clip generated from a single sentence

intro: Text to Video turns a short description of your product into a shooting script you can edit. You type one or two lines, press the Optimize button, and the composer hands back scenes, shots and a voice lined up as a brief.

Nothing renders while you read that brief. Every line stays editable, from the opening shot to the closing words, and the price appears once you settle on a version. Most first drafts need one pass to sharpen the claim and one to cut a repeating shot.
Reach for this tool when you have a product and a point to make, but no script. If photos or a product page already exist, a sibling tool saves the typing.

sections.h2: Where a sentence beats a photo
paras: Text to Video suits a claim you can say out loud: a serum that calms redness, a mat that stays put through a sprint. The brief supplies the shot order, the on-screen words and the voice. Photos can ground the scenes, but they never replace the sentence.

Pick a different tab when the raw material already exists. [AI Video](/guides/how-do-ai-video) starts from one to four product photos and keeps the item in frame; [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video) reads a public HTTPS product page and builds the brief from it. AI Image returns stills inline.

sections.h2: The sentence that starts everything
paras: Name three things in one or two lines: the product, the person you are talking to, and the single message they should leave with. A line carrying all three gives the composer a structure to fill. A slogan gives it nothing.

Compare "Give this moisturizer an honest review" with "Great results, amazing product". The first names an item, a tone and a job. The second could sit under any product on any shelf, so the scenes come back generic.
bullets: Product first: the exact item, not the category.
Audience second: who is deciding and what they already believe.
One message last: the claim the video has to land.
Leave out adjectives that would fit any competitor.

sections.h2: What you set before the quote
paras: Five controls decide what you pay for and what comes back: the Type selector, then model, aspect ratio, duration and resolution. Set them before you press Optimize, because each one shapes the brief the composer writes.

Then the quote. The confirmation window restates the estimated cost and your balance, and confirming holds the credits while the job runs. A failed job returns them automatically, with a plain-language reason and a Try again button. Save as draft costs nothing if the brief can wait.
bullets: Type keeps the job on Text to Video rather than a reference tab.
Aspect ratio decides the frame your shots are composed inside.
Duration sets the script length: 15 seconds costs 20 credits, 30 seconds costs 40.
Resolution sets how much detail the file keeps when it is re-cut.

sections.h2: Judging the result shot by shot
paras: Open the details modal for the finished video, the per-shot clips, the description, every reference you attached, and the submitted duration, aspect ratio and resolution. The per-shot clips show which scene missed, instead of letting the whole edit take the blame.

Separate the two kinds of failure before you spend anything. Retry render re-runs assembly while the existing clips stay untouched, which fits footage that is fine and joins that are not. Regenerate prefills the composer from the job, so rewrite the weak scene and keep the rest.

sections.h2: Where the file goes next
paras: Completed videos land in the Library under four filters: All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed. They stay for 15 days and then expire, so download the version you want to keep.

Captions come later, in [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio), and only for completed videos. Generate subtitles reads the actual speech, Promo lines and Product copy write on-screen text from your own words, and each operation stacks a new version over the player.

Publishing is one click to TikTok or Meta, or a download with no watermark. Keep the first paid clip narrow, one claim and one duration, so the next version has something honest to compare against. For the account side, see [the first TikTok video ad](/guides/first-tiktok-video-ad).

stepsIntro.title: Step by step
stepsIntro.lead: Six steps, and only one of them spends credits. The rest are reading, editing and checking, so a second pass over the brief is worth more than a second render.

steps.title: Write the sentence
steps.body: Start with the product, the person you are speaking to, and the one claim the video has to land. Keep it to one or two lines. If you cannot name the claim in a sentence, no script will fix that.

steps.title: Review the brief
steps.body: Press Optimize and read what comes back: scene order, the shot inside each scene, and the lines the voice will read. Change the wording or the order before anything runs. Keep the shots you can picture and rewrite the rest.

steps.title: Confirm the quote
steps.body: The confirmation window restates the estimated cost and your balance. Confirming holds the credits, with a 15-second video at 20 credits and a 30-second one at 40. Close the window if the number does not match the version on screen.

steps.title: Collect from the Library
steps.body: The job runs on the server, so you can leave the page while the badge moves through generating, finishing and completed. Open the details modal when it reads completed, watch the result and the per-shot clips, then download a copy before 15 days pass.

steps.title: Fix the scene that missed
steps.body: Compare the weak shot with the rest before you rerun anything. Retry render re-runs assembly when the clips themselves are fine. Regenerate prefills the composer from that job, so change the vague line in the brief before you run it again.

steps.title: Add captions before you export
steps.body: Subtitle Studio works on completed videos only, and each operation saves a new version while the original stays intact. Generate subtitles from the actual speech, or write product copy one line per screen. Download the version you prefer.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: A guest can build and save a draft without an account, and the draft is restored when the guest signs in. Drafts cost nothing, so you can rewrite the sentence as often as the claim changes.

checklist: The sentence names the product, the audience and one claim.
Every scene has a shot you can picture.
Aspect ratio and duration match where the video will run.
The quoted credits match the length you need.
You opened the per-shot clips before rerunning the job.

faq.q: How long should the first sentence be?
faq.a: One or two lines. Name the product, the one thing it does and who you are talking to. The composer expands that into scenes and voice, so length matters less than having a single claim to land.

faq.q: Can I edit the script before generating?
faq.a: Yes. The brief is fully editable: reorder scenes, rewrite lines, drop a shot. You confirm only the version you want to render, and the quote you approve belongs to that version.

faq.q: What happens if a job fails?
faq.a: You see a plain-language reason and a Try again button, and the held credits return automatically. There is no support ticket to file and no charge for the attempt.

intro: AI Video turns the product photos you already own into a short clip of a scene you describe. Attach them, write one moment, and the composer builds video where the product keeps its shape, colour and label from first frame to last.

The references do the steering, so this tool suits a product you can photograph from more than one side. A single photo, a plain sentence or a live product page each lead to a different route, and which route fits your material is the first decision.

Plan for two passes, not one. The first take shows you where the description was vague, and the second fixes it. Knowing what each reference steers, and how to word a single scene, usually saves you a whole third pass.

sections.h2: When references should drive the shot
paras: Choose AI Video when the product must look right in every shot: a printed logo, a specific label, a visible sole. You hold photos of it already, and the rest of the scene is what you invent.

Other tools cover different cases. One photo becomes motion in [Image to Video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video). A public product page is quicker in [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video), which pulls the product pictures for you.

The rule is about what you already hold. Photos from more than one side point here. If most of the clip is a person and the product appears only at the end, description carries the job and [Text to Video](/guides/how-do-text-to-video) is the lighter brief.

sections.h2: What each reference steers
paras: Photos fix the product. Attach one to four; each extra angle gives the model another side to read. Label text, the join of a strap and the taper of a bottle come from those pictures, not from your sentence.

On models that support them, two more slots appear. A reference video steers movement and camera behaviour. A reference audio sample steers the sound, so the take carries a tone. Slots belong to the model, so check them after a switch.
bullets: A product page screenshot leaves the label too soft to read.
A blurry angled phone shot teaches the model the blur as well.
A reference video with a quick cut invites that quick cut back.

sections.h2: A scene the model can finish
paras: One scene means one place, one subject and one thing happening. Name the room and the light, then the action: 'a hallway at eight, sun across the floor, she sets the tote down.' The model picks the camera move and the rhythm.

Leave the camera work out. Writing 'slow push-in, then a cut to the label' spends words on a decision the model makes better from one strong moment. A single action keeps the clip readable; a vague line such as 'show the bag being useful' gives no place, light or action.

sections.h2: What happens after you confirm
paras: Nothing runs until you confirm. The estimated cost appears as you change a reference or a duration: 20 credits for a 15-second video, 40 for 30 seconds. Edit an input and the figure can move, so read it once more before clicking.

The confirmation restates the estimate and your balance. Confirming holds the credits, and a failed job returns them on its own; the [refunds policy](/refunds) covers the rest. The job runs on the server, so leave the page and the Library badge catches up with "generating", "finishing" and "completed".

note.title: Two kinds of retry
note.body: Use "Retry render" when the clips are fine and only the assembly is wrong. Use "Regenerate" when the take drifted; it refills the composer from the job.

sections.h2: Comparing two takes of one brief
paras: Run the same brief again without editing it, then open both takes in the Library. Watch the opening two seconds and the shot where the product sits closest. Check the label, the strap and the light you asked for.

Open the details modal and the per-shot clips settle it. One weak shot with the rest holding is an assembly problem. A drift across every shot is a brief problem, and the description needs a sharper place or action.

Finished videos stay in the Library for 15 days, so download the keeper the day you choose it. Publish to TikTok or Meta in one click, or download without a watermark and size the crop with [ad sizes by platform](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform).

steps.title: Attach 2–3 references
steps.body: Open the AI Video tab and add your photos, up to four. Choose angles that answer different questions: the front label, the side seam, the product in a hand. Three frames of one corner teach the model nothing new.

steps.title: Describe one scene
steps.body: Name a place, a light and one action in a single line. 'Kitchen counter at seven, low sun, she sets the bottle down.' The model fills the camera move and the rhythm, so your words carry the moment rather than a shot list.

steps.title: Confirm the quote
steps.body: The cost updates as the duration or a reference changes. Before anything runs, the confirmation restates the estimate and your balance, and confirming holds the credits. A failed job lifts that hold on its own.

steps.title: Compare versions
steps.body: Run the brief again without editing it, then open both takes side by side. Judge the label, the strap and the light you asked for. Keep the stronger one; the other stays in the Library as a record of what changed.

steps.title: Read the job details
steps.body: Open the details modal on the take you are judging. It lists the result, the per-shot clips, your description, every reference you attached, and the duration, aspect ratio and resolution. The per-shot clips show which shot broke, if any.

stepsIntro.title: Step by step
stepsIntro.lead: The work follows the order the composer asks for it. Attach references, write one scene, read the quote, then compare what comes back. The last two steps are the ones most people skip, and both save a wasted pass.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: Keep one reference set for the whole comparison. Swap a photo halfway and the next take becomes a different product, not another edit, so the two versions stop answering the same question.

checklist: Two or three angles of one product, not near-identical frames.
A scene line with a place, a light and one action.
A model whose settings still show the reference slots you filled.
The quote read against the duration you want.
The per-shot clips watched before you judge a take.

faq.q: How many references should I attach?
faq.a: Two or three from different angles; the composer accepts one to four. Extra angles give the model more to read, so fewer surprises arrive between shots.

faq.q: Will my product stay consistent across shots?
faq.a: Every shot is built from the references you attached, so shape, colour and label detail follow that product. If a detail drifts, regenerate from the same references.

faq.q: What if a scene needs another take?
faq.a: Run the same brief again; both versions land in the Library and you keep the stronger one. If a job fails, a plain-language reason appears beside "Try again" and the held credits return.

faq.q: Do I need a reference video or audio?
faq.a: Only where the model offers those slots. Photos alone are enough to start; the extra slots help when movement or sound matters more than a still description. Switch models and check the row.

intro: AI Image turns a product photo into the stills a storefront and an ad account ask for. You choose a preset such as White background or Lifestyle photo, add a reference photo, and the page returns finished images with download links.

Buyers judge a listing by its main image long before they read anything. A clean white frame, one lifestyle shot and a crop that fits a paid placement cover most of the work, with the credit total visible before you commit.

Stills and video are different jobs. When the listing needs motion, a voice line or a multi-shot demo, the video tools do that better. Start here for images, then move on once the frame is right and you know which crop each channel wants.

sections.h2: When a still is the right output
paras: Reach for AI Image when the deliverable is a file someone will look at, not watch. A listing, a landing page tile and a product grid all take stills. When the listing needs motion, [image to video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video) turns a frame into a short demo.

The presets split the work by outcome. Custom image follows your description. White background strips the scene for listings. Change background keeps the product and swaps the setting. Lifestyle photo puts it in a real room, and Model photo adds a person holding or wearing it.

sections.h2: What the composer asks for
paras: Every run needs a short description, a preset, an aspect ratio and up to four reference photos. References anchor shape, colour and label; more is not automatically better. Two angles beat four near identical frames.

A usable reference is sharp, lit evenly and filled mostly by the product. Labels should read without glare, and the background should hold nothing that competes. If unsure what to send, start with [what a usable reference photo looks like](/guides/product-photo-tips).
bullets: Shoot on a plain surface in daylight, not on a coloured tablecloth
Fill the frame with one product and show its label straight on
Send the original file, not a screenshot or a stretched copy

sections.h2: From the quote to a finished file
paras: The price line sits above the button. Before a reference is attached it reads "Add a product reference photo to see the price". Attach one and it becomes "This generation costs N credits". A product photo costs 1 credit.

Edit the preset, the ratio or the number of references and the price moves. The button remembers the figure it last quoted, so it asks for a second click rather than charging the number you saw first.

Confirm and the modal restates the estimate beside your balance. Confirming holds the credits, and a failed job returns them on its own. The job runs on the server, so you can leave the tab and return to the result.

sections.h2: Judge the frame against the job
paras: Check the result the way a buyer will, as a thumbnail on a phone. Outline, label and product colour matter more than artistic detail. A frame showing a different item has failed, however good the picture looks.
When one part is wrong, fix that input and run the preset again. A wrong background points at the preset, a wrong shape at the reference photo, a wrong crop at the ratio.
bullets: Compare the result with the source photo at the same size
Zoom on the label; if you cannot read it, a buyer cannot either
Keep a frame only if the product profile is unchanged

sections.h2: Where the files go and what to build next
paras: Finished images appear inline on the page, each with a download link. They do not enter the video Library, so save the frames you keep before you close the tab. The Library holds video jobs, and videos stay there for 15 days.

Plan a set rather than a pile: one main image that carries the listing, one lifestyle frame that shows scale, and the crops your placements will buy. [Ad sizes by platform](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform) lists what each channel wants, and [white background rules](/guides/white-background-amazon) covers marketplace main images.

steps.title: Pick a tool preset
steps.body: Open the AI Image tab and choose the preset that matches the file you need. White background for a marketplace main image, Lifestyle photo for an ad that shows the product in use, Model photo when a person belongs in the frame.

steps.title: Set ratio and references
steps.body: Set the aspect ratio before you add photos, because it decides the crop. Then attach up to four references, starting with the clearest. Square suits a listing, tall suits stories, portrait suits a feed placement.

steps.title: Watch the price confirm
steps.body: Attach the first reference and the price line swaps its placeholder for a credit total. Change the preset, ratio or references after that and the total moves, so the button asks for a second click. Read the new figure, then confirm.

steps.title: Collect the results
steps.body: The run returns images inline on the page: a card shows the reserved credits while it works, then a download link when the file is ready. Nothing lands in the video Library. Judge each frame at thumbnail size first.

steps.title: Download the keepers
steps.body: Follow each download link and save the frames you will actually use. Keep the source photo beside them so you can explain later why a preset was chosen. A saved near miss is worth more than a repeat of the same idea.

steps.title: Run the crops a channel wants
steps.body: Return to the composer with the same preset and reference, change only the ratio, and confirm the new total. Each crop is its own run, so plan two or three, starting with the placement you have bought.

stepsIntro.title: Step by step
stepsIntro.lead: Six short moves take you from a product photo to a finished still. Work through them in order the first time, then repeat only the parts a new channel changes.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: Two references from different angles usually beat four that repeat one view. Change a single input between runs so you can tell which one helped.

checklist: Pick one preset per job and keep it fixed between runs
Read the price line again after any input change
Attach a sharp, evenly lit photo that fills the frame
Download every keeper; results do not enter the video Library
Plan a main image plus the crops your channels actually buy

faq.q: Can I get marketplace-ready white background images?
faq.a: Yes. The White background preset strips the scene and keeps the product, which is what a listing main image needs. Check the marketplace rules on the frame, then read the field guide on white background requirements.

faq.q: Do I need professional photos to start?
faq.a: No. Clear phone photos on a plain surface are enough as references. The preset copies shape, colour and label from what you supply, so sharpness and even light matter more than the camera.

faq.q: Can I make social crops of the same image?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the cheapest way to finish a set. Run the same preset and reference with a different ratio, confirm the new total, and download the crop. Squares suit listings, tall frames suit stories.

faq.q: Do generated images appear in the Library?
faq.a: No. AI Image results stay on the page with their download links, so nothing waits in the Library. Video jobs live there instead, and videos expire after 15 days. Save what you intend to keep.

intro: A product you sell on five channels should not need fresh photos for every brief. Product Links keeps each product once, as a card that carries a thumbnail, the description the page published and the source host it came from.

Import once, then generate many. The same card works next month: press "Create your video" and the product details and photos travel into the panel, so the fifth ad costs an edit rather than a search through old export files.

The library becomes the working memory of your shop. Corrections you make on a card stay there, retired items leave the shelf, and a tidy set of cards turns each later brief into a quick choice instead of a guess.

sections.h2: The library behind every brief
paras: A card is not a file dump. Each entry holds one product: a thumbnail you recognise, the description the import read, and the host it came from, which is how you spot a card pulled from the wrong shop.

Not every job needs a card. If you will brief one page once and never again, send it straight through [URL to Video](/guides/how-do-url-to-video). Where no product page exists yet, [AI Video](/guides/how-do-ai-video) builds the ad from photos you already own.
Growth is the real test of a library. Two hundred unnamed cards help nobody; twenty you can still describe make a month of briefs feel short, so delete what you have stopped selling.

sections.h2: What makes a good import
paras: The import needs a public HTTPS product page: your own shop, a marketplace listing, or a landing page. It reads the title, description and images already published there, and a price when the page shows one.

Strong input looks like a shop page: several photos of one item, a description naming material or size, and a price. A thin page produces a card you finish by hand, and [product photo tips](/guides/product-photo-tips) show which frames are worth keeping.
bullets: Photos show one product, not a grid of the catalogue
A description that names material, size or colour
Page stays public, with no sign-in step
One product per page, not a range in one listing

sections.h2: From card to running job
paras: The scrape preview tells you what to trust. It shows the sourced title, description, detected images and a possible price, each with a confidence label, and a possible price is never treated as confirmed.

Press "Create your video" on the card and the panel opens inline with the product attached. Set duration and aspect ratio for your placement, then read the estimate before you confirm: 20 credits for 15 seconds, 40 for 30 seconds. [Ad sizes by platform](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform) lists the common ones.

Confirming holds the credits, and the modal restates the estimated cost and your current balance. The banner reads "Generating your video", then "Your video is ready", with Download and Open Library buttons.

note.title: While it runs
note.body: The job runs on the server, so you can leave the page; the Library badge updates when you return.

sections.h2: Fixing a card that reads wrong
paras: Open the card before you brief it and check what the brief depends on: photos that show the item, a description you would use, the correct source host. Where the scrape fell short, backfill by hand, and what you save is what later briefs use.

When the product page itself changes, re-import the same URL. New photography or rewritten copy belongs on the card, and nothing moves until you import again, so the library never changes behind your back.
checklist: Card photos show the product, not a packaging shot
Description names the material or size you advertise
Source host is the shop you actually sell from
No card left behind for a product you have dropped

sections.h2: After the banner says ready
paras: A finished video waits in the Library for 15 days, then expires. Download what you want to keep, or publish to TikTok or Meta in one click; a download carries no watermark.

Captions and on-screen text come later, in [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio), which works on completed videos only. Each operation saves a new version, the original stays untouched, and versions stack as tabs over the player.
The card stays useful after that. Keep it current, and the next ad starts from work you already did, one click from the shelf you keep tidy rather than a folder you rebuild.

steps.title: Import products
steps.body: Paste the product page URL and let the import read it. The entry saves with a thumbnail, description and source host, so the same product never needs a second upload for the next ad. Start with the items you advertise most.

steps.title: Manage the library
steps.body: Open a card when it looks thin and backfill the photos or description the scrape missed. Delete entries you no longer sell, because a long shelf of dead products slows every visit you make to it.

steps.title: Create from a card
steps.body: Press "Create your video" on the card and the panel builds the video inline, with the product photos already attached. Read the estimated cost, confirm, and the banner tracks the run to "Your video is ready".

steps.title: Refresh a stale card
steps.body: When the shop page has new photography or new copy, re-import the same URL instead of patching the card by hand. Nothing on the card changes until you import, which keeps old briefs and new ones consistent.

steps.title: Check the result
steps.body: Open the Library and filter to Completed, then open the details modal for the video, per-shot clips, the description and every reference you attached. If the clips are fine but the assembly is wrong, use Retry render; for a different take, Regenerate prefills the panel.

stepsIntro.title: Step by step
stepsIntro.lead: Five steps take you from a product page to a video you can publish. The first two build the shelf, the last three use it, and each one is shorter once the card is already in place.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: Re-import is the fix for a changed page, not for a changed card. If you only want a different lead photo or shorter copy, edit the card directly, and keep the URL for the day the shop rewrites the page.

checklist: One card per product, for items you still sell
Product photos on the card show the item alone
Description names the material, size or colour you sell
Source host points at the shop you use
Dead products deleted rather than left to clutter the shelf

faq.q: Which product pages can I import from?
faq.a: Any public HTTPS product page works: your own shop, a marketplace listing or a landing page. The import reads the photos and description already on the page, and blocked pages return a specific reason.

faq.q: Can I fix things after the import?
faq.a: Yes. Open the card and backfill what the scrape missed: a photo, a description that skipped the material, or a source host pointing at the wrong shop. What you save is what future briefs use.

faq.q: What happens when my product page changes?
faq.a: Import the URL again and the card picks up the new photography and copy. Nothing in your library changes until you do, so a card never rewrites itself between briefs.

howto.h1: Present your product with an AI avatar.
howto.lead: Choose a presenter, paste your script, and generate a talking product video — no filming, no studio, and the same face across every video you publish.

image.alt: Jon, an outdoor AI actor presenter card

intro: An AI avatar is a presenter who reads your script on camera without a shoot, a studio or anyone in front of a lens. You attach the product photos, cast the face and voice, and the video comes back with the item in hand.

Not every product needs a voice. A single photo that should move belongs in [Image to Video](/guides/how-do-image-to-video), and a scene built from several product shots belongs in [AI Video](/guides/how-do-ai-video). Reach for the presenter when the value of the item has to be explained out loud.
Three decisions shape the result: which presenter, which words, which format. None of them is a setting you can fix in the edit. Get them right and the rest is confirmation and waiting.

sections.h2: When a presenter carries the story
paras: A talking presenter suits products that need explaining: why the fabric holds, how the strap adjusts, what fits inside the bag. Casting sets the tone, because a calm delivery suits an everyday product and reads flat on a launch. The face gives the viewer someone to follow while the script sells.

The usual failure is a presenter describing something the viewer cannot see. Small items and dark items need the hands and the placement to do more work, and no voice fixes a product that stays out of frame.

sections.h2: What the workspace asks for
paras: You provide product photos, a presenter and a script. The picker holds 53 available avatars with filters for All, Women and Men, plus search by name, character or scene. Each card previews the voice and a sample line.
Photos decide how the hands look. Send the item alone on a plain surface, with front and back both sharp enough to read on a phone. Two clear angles beat five near identical shots.
bullets: One frame for each side the viewer will see in the cut.
Even light on the product, so the colour holds in the cut.
A close shot of the detail the script points at, so it survives a thumbnail.

sections.h2: From quote to finished job
paras: Your cost appears before anything runs, and the confirmation modal restates the estimate beside your current balance. A 15-second video costs 20 credits and a 30-second video costs 40. Confirming holds the credits until the job settles.

Server-side, the job runs while you do something else. Close the tab if you like, because the Library badge moves from generating to finishing to completed while you are away. A failed render returns the credits automatically, with no support ticket.

note.title: Nothing is spent until it runs
note.body: Confirming holds the credits, and a failed job hands them back. A draft costs nothing and is restored when a guest signs in.

sections.h2: Reading the result honestly
paras: Watch the opening with the sound off, then again with it on. If the product is not visible and in use by the end of the first line, later frames rarely recover the viewer.

Sort the fault before you spend again. A voice that does not fit, a face with the wrong energy, or hands that grip the item badly are casting problems. Another presenter fixes all three. Broken joins are assembly problems, so Retry render re-runs assembly when the clips are sound.
When the words are the fault, Regenerate prefills the composer from the job. That keeps the presenter and the photos in place while you rewrite only the line that failed.

sections.h2: Keeping the file and the cuts
paras: Finished videos sit in the Library for 15 days, then expire, so download what you keep. Filters for All videos, In progress, Failed and Completed sort the list, and the details modal shows the result and every reference you attached.

Keep one presenter for a campaign and test the script instead of the face. A viewer who meets the same person three times recognises the ad before the product name appears, while a new actor each time starts the introduction over.

Captions come after the cut. [Subtitle Studio](/guides/how-do-subtitle-studio) works on completed videos only. Each operation saves a new version and leaves the original untouched. Captions from the actual speech follow the delivery, while Product copy puts your own lines on screen.

steps.title: Attach product references
steps.body: Add the photos the presenter will hold, wear or demonstrate. Front and back views on a plain surface give the hands somewhere to land, and the detail the script mentions should be readable in the frame.

steps.title: Choose a presenter
steps.body: Filter All, Women or Men, or search by name, character or scene. Each card previews the voice and a sample line, so you hear the delivery before you cast. My avatars accepts a portrait you upload instead.

steps.title: Write the script
steps.body: Scripts run up to 5,000 characters, more room than a short video needs. Write spoken sentences, one idea each, and read them aloud before you paste. A line that takes two breaths will sound rushed.

steps.title: Quote, confirm, generate
steps.body: Set the format, the duration and the spoken language first, then read the cost and confirm. The modal restates the estimate against your balance, and held credits return on their own if the render fails.

steps.title: Check the cut before you download
steps.body: Play it once with the sound off to check the product, then with sound on to check the voice. If the clips are fine and the joins are not, use Retry render. If the casting is wrong, use Regenerate.

stepsIntro.title: Step by step
stepsIntro.lead: Five steps take you from photos to a finished presenter video. The first three decide how the result looks, and the last two decide whether the video is worth keeping.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: Hear the sample line on two or three cards before you cast. A voice that reads well can land differently once it speaks your own lines, so the card is the cheapest place to find out.

checklist: Product visible and in use by the end of the opening line.
Presenter and voice suit the placement, not only the product.
Every spoken sentence fits one breath without a rush.
Format, duration and language match where the video runs.
One presenter carries every video in the campaign.
Files downloaded before the 15-day Library window closes.

faq.q: Can I use the same presenter across videos?
faq.a: Yes, and it is worth doing. One presenter keeps the face and the voice consistent, so viewers recognise the ads before the product name appears. Change the script and the placement, not the actor.

faq.q: Can I choose the spoken language per video?
faq.a: Yes. The spoken language is set per video, so one presenter can address different markets without a new cast. Match it to where the video will run, and hear the voice preview before you confirm.

faq.q: Can I use my own face instead of the library?
faq.a: My avatars accepts a portrait you upload, so your own presenter sits beside the 53 built-in ones. Use a clear, evenly lit photo of the face you want, and reuse the same image across the campaign.

faq.q: What happens if a job fails?
faq.a: The job gives a plain reason and a Try again action, and the held credits return automatically. Retry render re-runs assembly when the clips are fine; Regenerate prefills the composer when the script needs a change.

howto.h1: Subtitle a finished video in minutes.
howto.lead: Pick a finished video, choose the operation, and style the captions with a live preview — then burn in a new version, ready for silent autoplay feeds.

image.alt: Video frame with styled subtitles burned in

intro: Subtitle Studio takes a video you have already finished and gives it captions. Nothing is re-shot: you pick an existing job from the list and the tool writes a second cut beside it. The version you approved stays exactly as it was.

Most feeds play with the sound off, so the caption line is often the only thing a viewer reads before scrolling. A silent autoplay feed turns spoken words into on-screen text. A clip that opens with a line nobody can hear has no argument.

You can caption the speech in the video, or set your own words for each screen. Either way you choose the look, check the sample preview, and keep both cuts. The steps below cover the operations, the style choices, and how to pick the better version.

sections.h2: Captions carry a silent feed
paras: A muted feed removes your voice track and leaves the picture. Viewers still decide within a second whether the clip is for them, and words on screen are the fastest thing to read. Captions turn a spoken line into a visible claim.

Reach for this tool when the footage is settled and the words need work. If the shots are wrong, go back to the composer: the [AI Video guide](/guides/how-do-ai-video) covers a fresh render. Captions repair a silent cut, not a dull one.

sections.h2: What each operation asks of you
paras: Generate subtitles reads the speech in the video and turns it into captions, so you bring nothing but the finished clip. Promo lines and Product copy take text you write, each line becoming one screen. A pasted paragraph arrives as one crowded line.

Good input is short. Write one idea per line, each short enough to read in a breath. Three tight lines beat a full script, and [the AI UGC video ads guide](/blog/ai-ugc-video-ads-guide) shows how an opening works.
bullets: Generate subtitles when the spoken script is already right.
Promo lines for a short hook laid over the footage.
Product copy when on-screen text must name the item.

sections.h2: Preview, then save a version
paras: Pick the video from the list on the left, narrowing it with a word from the prompt or the title. Choose the operation, then set Style, Size, Position, Colour and Backdrop. The sample caption preview updates as you change each control.

Starting the job saves a new version instead of overwriting the file you selected. The original keeps its Library entry and the captioned cut arrives beside it. Leave the page while the job runs; the badge updates when you return.

note.title: One control at a time
note.body: Moving Size, Position and Backdrop together leaves you unsure which one fixed the line. Change one setting, watch the preview, then decide.

sections.h2: A caption that runs past the screen
paras: A line is too long when the preview wraps or reaches the edges before the sentence ends. On a phone the limit is how often the eye jumps back to the start, not the character count. If reading it aloud leaves you behind, the line is long.

Three clean repairs: cut the line to its subject and verb, split it across two screens, or raise Size a step and drop it to the bottom. Change one thing, then watch the preview. Style combinations that hold up stay legible over moving footage.
bullets: Bold with a box backdrop holds up over busy product shots.
White text with an outline survives pale walls and daylight.
Bottom position keeps faces and hands clear on a vertical crop.

sections.h2: Comparing versions before you post
paras: Versions stack as tabs above the player. Switch between them at the same timestamp, sound off, and ask which answers a buyer's first question. A line that reads well on a desktop can vanish into a busy phone frame, so check the crop you will post.

Keep the tab you trust, download it, and publish. Finished videos stay in the Library for 15 days, so download what you want to keep. Crops for each placement sit in [ad sizes by platform](/guides/ad-sizes-by-platform), with [the review checklist](/blog/ai-video-review-checklist) for the rest.

steps.title: Pick a finished video
steps.body: Open Subtitle Studio and choose a completed job from the list on the left. Search by a word from the prompt or the title when the list is long. Only finished videos appear, because the tool works on footage that already exists.

steps.title: Choose an operation
steps.body: Choose Generate subtitles to caption the speech in the video, or Promo lines and Product copy to set your own text. For the text operations, write one line per screen. The operation sets the words; the style controls set the look.

steps.title: Style it with live preview
steps.body: Set Style, Size, Position, Colour and Backdrop and watch the sample caption preview change. Change one control at a time so you can tell which one helped. Judge the line against the busiest frame.

steps.title: Generate a new version
steps.body: Start the job and the tool saves the styled cut as a new version beside the original. Nothing is overwritten, so the approved video stays in the Library. Leave the page if you need to; the badge updates later.

steps.title: Compare the two tabs
steps.body: Switch between the version tabs at the same moment in the clip and watch both with the sound off. Judge the opening line, the longest line, and the final frame. Note one thing each version does better.

steps.title: Download or publish
steps.body: Download the version you chose, or publish it to TikTok or Meta from the workspace. Downloads carry no watermark, and the Library copy expires after 15 days, so keep your own file.

stepsIntro.title: Six steps on one finished video
stepsIntro.lead: Every step leaves the earlier cut intact, so a poor style choice costs a second version rather than the video you approved. Work the list once, then compare the tabs.

tip.title: Good to know
tip.body: Copy written for reading lands better than copy written for speaking: cut the filler and let the picture carry the rest. Two versions are enough; a third makes choosing harder.

checklist: The video you open is completed, not still running.
Each on-screen line fits one screen in the preview.
Style, Size and Backdrop were checked on the busiest frame.
Both versions were watched muted at the same timestamp.
The chosen version is downloaded before the 15 days end.

faq.q: Will the original video change?
faq.a: No. Every operation saves a new version, and the video you picked keeps its own entry in the Library. Versions stack as tabs over the player, so the first cut stays available.

faq.q: What can a new version contain?
faq.a: The operations are Generate subtitles, Promo lines and Product copy. Generate subtitles captions the speech already in the video; the other two set your own words, one line per screen. Captions keep the language of the audio.

faq.q: Which style reads best on mobile?
faq.a: Bold type with a box or outline backdrop in the bottom third is the safest start, because it survives busy footage and pale backgrounds. Check the preview at Medium before going larger. Middle suits one short line.

faq.q: How long do the versions stay?
faq.a: Finished videos sit in the Library for 15 days, then expire, versions included. Download the cut you plan to post and keep your own copy of anything you reuse.
